Cell Growth Curve and Concentration Response Analysis

Zachery Moore

22 October 2026

Contents

1 Objective

The dosefitr package provides tools for analysing cell growth curves and the subsequenet calculation of doubling rates. This vignette walks through the main functionality using an example dataset included with the package.

2 Loading and visualising data

First, load the package.

library(dosefitr)

The double_data dataset contains longitudinal measurements of spheroid area, acquired on the IncuCyte, at two seeding densities (1000 and 2000 cells). We start by plotting area over time, coloured by seeding density.

data("double_data", package = "dosefitr")

double_data_filt <- double_data |>
  dplyr::select(cells_seeded, hours_from, area)

ggplot2::ggplot(
  double_data_filt,
  ggplot2::aes(hours_from, area, colour = as.factor(cells_seeded))
) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::labs(colour = "Cells seeded")

Both seeding densities show the expected exponential growth, with the higher density (2000 cells) reaching larger final areas than the lower density (1000 cells).

3 Fitting growth models

fit_curve() fits a growth model to the data. Here we use five_param_sigmoid. Parameters can be shared between experimental groups to improve fitting stability: shared_group specifies the column holding the grouping variable (seeding density), and shared_parameters specifies which model parameters are shared. Here we share top (maximum growth) and slope.

double_model <- fit_curve(
  data = double_data_filt,
  x_var = "hours_from",
  y_var = "area",
  curve_options = list(model = "five_param_sigmoid"),
  shared_options = list(
    shared_group = "cells_seeded",
    shared_parameters = c("top", "slope")
  )
)

The fitted nls object contains the parameter estimates for each curve.

double_model$curve$nls_model
## Nonlinear regression model
##   model: y ~ f(x, top, slope, bottom_1000, bottom_2000, s_1000, s_2000,     ec50_1000, ec50_2000, group)
##    data: data
##         top       slope bottom_1000   ec50_1000      s_1000 bottom_2000 
##   1.799e+05   8.569e+00   3.187e+04   2.657e+02   1.484e-01   5.969e+04 
##   ec50_2000      s_2000 
##   1.415e+02   1.435e-01 
##  residual sum-of-squares: 5.126e+11
## 
## Number of iterations till stop: 50 
## Achieved convergence tolerance: 1.49e-08
## Reason stopped: Number of iterations has reached `maxiter' == 50.

We can then visualise the fit.

plot_model(
  list = double_model,
  x_var = "hours_from",
  y_var = "area"
)

4 Handling outliers

Experimental data often contain outliers that can distort model fits. Setting huber = TRUE uses a Huber loss to down-weight the influence of extreme points during fitting, and rout = TRUE uses the ROUT method to identify and remove outliers. Outliers are highlighted in the resulting plot.

double_model_outlier <- fit_curve(
  data = double_data_filt,
  x_var = "hours_from",
  y_var = "area",
  curve_options = list(model = "five_param_sigmoid"),
  shared_options = list(
    shared_group = "cells_seeded",
    shared_parameters = c("top", "slope")
  ),
  outlier_options = list(huber = TRUE, rout = TRUE)
)

plot_model(
  list = double_model_outlier,
  x_var = "hours_from",
  y_var = "area"
)

5 Calculating doubling times

Doubling time is a key metric for growth analysis. We first use predict_data() to generate smooth predicted curves from the fitted model for each seeding density.

double_model_predicted <- lapply(
  c(1000, 2000),
  function(group) {
    predict_data(
      nls_model = double_model$curve$nls_model,
      lower_x = min(double_model$data$hours_from),
      upper_x = max(double_model$data$hours_from),
      group = group
    )
  }
) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  dplyr::rename(hours_from = x, area = y, cells_seeded = group)

calc_double_rate_data() then calculates the doubling time from these predicted curves. Because spheroid area is a two-dimensional readout of a three-dimensional object, doubling_readout_factor converts the area change to the equivalent change in volume (here 2^(2/3), assuming spherical spheroids). For confluence or direct cell counts, set this to 1. The function also returns diagnostic plots showing the growth curves and the points used in the calculation.

double_rate <- calc_double_rate_data(
  data = double_model_predicted,
  x_var = "hours_from",
  y_var = "area",
  cell_column = "cells_seeded",
  doubling_readout_factor = 2^(2 / 3)
)

# Diagnostic plots
double_rate$linear

double_rate$log

# Doubling time
double_rate$double_time
## [1] 87.66387
